title: API 510 Training in Toledo, OH: Vessel Inspector Exam Prep
description: API 510 exam prep for Toledo, Oregon and Lima vessel inspectors: hydrocracker, reformer and coker vessels, Ohio special inspectors, self-paced online.
h1: API 510 training in Toledo: exam preparation for pressure vessel inspectors at the Oregon and Lima refineries and the plants of north-west Ohio
html:
API 510 exam prep for pressure vessel inspectors in Toledo and north-west Ohio

Most of the API 510 work within reach of Toledo sits in four refineries: two just outside the city, one at Lima to the south and one in Detroit to the north. Between them they run crude and vacuum columns, hydrocracker and reformer reactors, coke drums and fractionators, alkylation and amine vessels and long banks of shell-and-tube exchangers. Each of those vessels has a thickness history, a governing component and a date by which somebody must decide whether it can run another cycle. Making that decision, and defending it with the code, is what the API 510 Pressure Vessel Inspector certification is about.

Atlantis NDT's API 510 course prepares you for the examination. It is self-paced and online: you begin when you enrol, move through the material in the order and at the speed your shifts allow, and send questions to an instructor who answers them from the code text. There is no Atlantis classroom in Toledo; Atlantis has offices in Houston and Hyderabad, and the whole course runs on its learning portal. The American Petroleum Institute decides who is eligible, administers the examination at Prometric test centres and issues the certification to those who pass.

Four refineries, read through EIA's unit figures

The U.S. Energy Information Administration's 2026 Refinery Capacity Report lists every operable refinery as of the start of the year, unit by unit and under its current owner. For a vessel inspector the downstream columns say more than the crude number, because each unit type brings its own vessels and its own damage.

Marathon Petroleum Co LP, Detroit146,000 b/cdVacuum distillation 90,500; delayed coking 40,500; diesel desulfurization 51,000; asphalt 32,000435

Read the last column first. Sulfur recovery capacity is a fair guide to how much sulfur a refinery's crude slate brings in, and the two plants beside Toledo sit far apart on it. PBF describes its refinery, on a 282-acre site with a Nelson complexity of 11.0, as running light, sweet crudes from Canada, the Mid-continent, the Bakken and the Gulf Coast, and its sulfur capacity is about a quarter of its neighbour's. Cenovus's Oregon refinery, which the company says opened in 1919 and which today makes asphalt, coke and sulfur alongside its fuels, carries a delayed coker and a large vacuum unit. An inspector who moves between the two sites changes damage picture, not just badge.

Lima adds a third pattern. Cenovus calls it the longest-running continuously operating oil refinery in the United States, in service since 1886, and its EIA entry shows coking, hydrocracking, high-pressure reforming and an aromatics plant. Marathon's Detroit refinery, about 60 miles north (PBF places its own site 60 miles south of Detroit), is a coking refinery with large asphalt capacity. The owner-user inspection groups at these four plants, and the contractors who staff their turnarounds, hold most of the full-time API 510 work around Toledo.

What these units put on a Toledo vessel inspector's list

The current API 510 Body of Knowledge examines fifteen damage mechanism paragraphs of API RP 571, plus its definitions, and nothing else from that document. Mapped onto the units in the table, they fall into four groups.

Hydrogen service: hydrocrackers and reformers

All three Ohio refineries run hydrocrackers and reformers, so high-temperature hydrogen attack (RP 571, 3.36) and high-temperature H2/H2S corrosion (3.35) are the mechanisms most likely to drive inspection planning on reactor circuits. HTHA is the one candidates struggle with, because it gives so little surface warning: learn what drives it, which steels RP 571 associates with it and why finding it is specialist work rather than routine thickness gauging. Reformers carry a second trap. Chlorides from the catalyst and its regeneration can show up as hydrochloric acid corrosion (3.37) in effluent and stabiliser equipment, not only in the crude unit overhead where most people expect to meet HCl.

Sour service: amine, sour water and the coker

Where sulfur capacity is high, so is the population of vessels in wet H2S service: amine contactors and regenerators, sour water strippers, coker and catalytic cracker fractionator overhead drums. Wet H2S damage (3.67), in its blistering, HIC, SOHIC and SSC forms, and amine stress corrosion cracking (3.3) belong here, with sulfidation (3.61) in the hot sections of crude, vacuum and coking units. Naphthenic acid corrosion (3.46) is on the list as well; whether it matters at a particular site depends on the crudes that site buys.

Water, steam and caustic

Every refinery runs a steam system, and its deaerators, condensate drums and blowdown vessels are pressure vessels with their own mechanism, boiler water and steam condensate corrosion (3.9). Caustic corrosion and caustic stress corrosion cracking (3.14 and 3.15) apply wherever caustic is used for treating or neutralising, and chloride stress corrosion cracking (3.17) to austenitic stainless shells, internals and exchanger tubing.

Weather, insulation and flow

Lake Erie winters make brittle fracture (3.11) a practical question on thick vessels that are started up cold or hydrotested in the colder months, and freeze-thaw cycling drives corrosion under insulation (3.22) and atmospheric corrosion (3.8). Erosion and erosion-corrosion (3.27) complete the fifteen.

Two concerns a Toledo candidate meets on these units are missing from that list. Temper embrittlement of chrome-moly hydroprocessing reactors, and the polythionic acid cracking that sensitised stainless equipment can suffer at shutdown, are both real on hydrogen units, but neither appears among the RP 571 paragraphs the current Body of Knowledge names, so treat them as job knowledge rather than exam content. Check the list for your own window, because API revises it.

Exchangers, steam drums and deaerators: where API 510 meets Ohio's boiler rules

Ohio regulates boilers and pressure vessels through two sets of rules. The Board of Building Standards writes the rules for construction, installation, repair and operation in Ohio Administrative Code chapters 4101:4-1 to 4101:4-10, and rule 4101:4-2-01 says in-service inspections are carried out by general and special inspectors under rules the superintendent of the Division of Industrial Compliance adopts in chapter 1301:3-5. That chapter, administered within the Ohio Department of Commerce, is built around boilers: power boilers are inspected internally and externally at intervals of not more than one year, process boilers at not more than three, and an owner may apply in writing for a longer interval with supporting information and an inspector's report. Under Revised Code section 4104.15 the superintendent issues the certificate of operation once the owner or user has met those requirements.

The inspector definitions matter to anyone working in a refinery inspection department. A general inspector is a State of Ohio employee. A special inspector holds a National Board commission and an Ohio commission and usually works for an insurer, but the definition in rule 4101:4-1-01 also lets an owner-user employ one, provided the owner-user maintains an inspection programme meeting the National Board's NB-371 rules for owner-user inspection organisations; while acting as a special inspector, that person represents the state and acts independently of the employer. An API 510 certificate is not an Ohio commission and replaces nothing in that system. It shows that you know the in-service code most refinery vessel programmes are written around, and some inspectors in owner-user programmes hold both.

The same definitions name categories older plants still meet. An "Ohio-standard" vessel was built to the former Ohio industrial commission rules but never ASME-stamped, an "Ohio special" was approved by special action of the Board although it does not fully comply with ASME, and a "non-standard" vessel was installed before July 1913 without stamping to Ohio rules. None of this is API 510 exam material, but in a state where one refinery has run since 1886 it helps to know these labels exist when a nameplate does not look the way a textbook says it should.

Exchangers deserve their own note. Plants around Toledo run a great many of them, and the Body of Knowledge reflects that: ASME PCC-2 Article 312, on inspection and repair of shell-and-tube heat exchangers, is examined alongside API RP 572 on vessel inspection practice, while the tubesheet calculations of Section VIII Part UHX are excluded. Expect questions about how exchangers are inspected, plugged, retubed and repaired, not about how they were designed. Background reading: heat exchanger tube inspection methods.

Worked example: an ellipsoidal head, the next interval and MAWP for the next run

Head questions are where many candidates expect easy marks and drop them, because the interval rule and the MAWP rule interlock. Take a hydrotreater or reformer separator with 2:1 ellipsoidal heads, inside diameter 72 in. and design pressure 250 psig. The problem gives an allowable stress of 20,000 psi and a joint efficiency of 1.0 for a seamless head, and there is no static head to add.

  1. Required thickness of a 2:1 ellipsoidal head under UG-32: t = PD ÷ (2SE − 0.2P) = (250 × 72) ÷ (40,000 − 50) = 18,000 ÷ 39,950 = 0.451 in.
  2. Readings at the head knuckle CML: 0.625 in. sixteen years ago, 0.595 in. eight years ago and 0.535 in. today. Long-term rate = 0.090 ÷ 16 = 0.0056 in. per year; short-term rate = 0.060 ÷ 8 = 0.0075 in. per year. The faster short-term rate followed a change of feed and reflects current conditions, so it governs.
  3. Remaining corrosion allowance = 0.535 − 0.451 = 0.084 in., and remaining life = 0.084 ÷ 0.0075 = 11.3 years.
  4. Internal or on-stream interval: the lesser of half the remaining life and 10 years, which gives 5.6 years.
  5. MAWP for continued service: API 510 uses the measured thickness minus twice the corrosion expected before the next inspection. For a five-year run that is 0.535 − 2 × (0.0075 × 5) = 0.460 in., and P = 2SEt ÷ (D + 0.2t) = 18,400 ÷ 72.09 = 255 psi, comfortably above the 250 psig design pressure.

Now run the same numbers over the full 5.6 years. The thickness used becomes 0.535 − 2 × 0.042 = 0.451 in., the required thickness again, and the MAWP comes out at 250 psi exactly. That is not a coincidence: subtracting twice the loss over half the remaining life removes the entire remaining corrosion allowance, so the two rules are built to meet at the same point. The trap sits on the other side. Use the slower long-term rate and the remaining life stretches to 15 years and the interval to 7.5, a tidy-looking option that hides a vessel now losing metal faster than it used to. For the code itself, the API 510 code explainer is a useful companion.

Who sits API 510 around Toledo, and how the experience adds up

API counts education plus pressure vessel experience gained within the last ten years while employed by, or under contract with, an authorized inspection agency, which includes an owner-user inspection organisation. A bachelor's degree in engineering or technology needs one year supervising or performing inspection; a two-year degree or certificate needs two years, one of them in inspection; a high school diploma needs three; no formal education needs five or more. The API 510 certification requirements page sets the rules out in full. Around Toledo, candidates usually arrive by one of four routes.

  • NDT technicians. Thickness gaugers and weld inspectors on refinery contracts build vessel experience quickly, and the inspection year starts to accrue when they evaluate readings rather than only take them. NDT training in Toledo covers the ASNT SNT-TC-1A route into that work.
  • Welders and boilermakers. Owens Community College offers a welding associate degree and a pipe welding certificate. Fabrication and repair years count towards the total, and whether a particular associate degree counts as engineering or technology education is API's decision when it reviews your application.
  • Operators. Board and outside operators often know their unit's vessels better than anyone on site. Operating years count towards the longer routes, but the inspection year still has to be earned in an inspection role.
  • Engineers. The University of Toledo requires its engineering science students to complete three semester-long paid co-ops, starting in the second year. A placement in a refinery inspection or reliability group is a strong start; whether any co-op time counts towards the experience requirement is for API to decide from your record.

Three or more years of technical military service count like a bachelor's degree, unless the discharge was dishonorable. Keep your own log of the vessels you inspect and the tasks you perform, because API verifies the experience you document.

Studying for API 510 around Oregon and Lima turnarounds

Refinery inspection around Toledo follows the rhythm of turnarounds and of a winter that slows outdoor work, and most candidates plan their study around both rather than against them. Self-paced study suits that pattern: you stop for the weeks of twelve-hour turnaround shifts and resume at the lesson where the portal left you, with nobody moving on without you. A sequence that works for many people:

  1. API 510 itself. Read it through once, then learn the interval, corrosion rate and remaining life rules well enough to answer without the book, because the Body of Knowledge says those formulas may be closed-book.
  2. Section VIII, by the Body of Knowledge list. Shells and heads under UG-27 and UG-32, joint efficiency from UW-11 and UW-12, static head, test pressure under UG-99 and UG-100, impact test exemption under UCS-66 and weld sizes at openings. Ignore the parts the BOK excludes.
  3. RP 571, mapped onto your own unit. Take each of the fifteen paragraphs and find one vessel at your site where it applies. A mechanism you can picture on a real drum is far easier to recall in the closed-book half.
  4. Section IX and RP 577. Practise reviewing a WPS against its PQR until checking variables becomes routine.
  5. Timed papers. Finish with papers that copy the real split, then send the instructor every question you got right for the wrong reason.

Bring questions from the job as well. An exchanger nameplate with a radiography marking you cannot read, a rerate letter in an old file, or a PCC-2 repair you watched being planned all make good questions, and the instructor answers each one from the code text so you learn where the answer lives as well as what it is.

Sitting the API 510 exam from Toledo

API 510 is taken in person on a single day, and Prometric lists test centres in and around Toledo; candidates from Lima or from across the Michigan line pick whichever centre suits them once API has accepted the application. The day runs to 7.5 hours: a short tutorial, 110 closed-book questions in 2.75 hours, a 45-minute lunch break, then 60 open-book questions in 3.75 hours. Of the 170 questions, 140 are scored and 30 are unscored pretest items you cannot tell apart. In the open-book half the examined codes are PDFs on the screen, and you may not bring papers, notes or books. API runs the exam in set windows during the year, each with its own application deadline, listed on the API exam schedule page.

Ways to prepare from Toledo, compared

  • Concentrated seminars. Several training companies run intensive API 510 seminars ahead of exam windows, in person in other cities or online at fixed times. They suit candidates who already know the codes and can be released for the dates.
  • Employer mentoring. Owner-user groups at the larger refineries bring on their own people, which teaches site procedures, inspection software and local history as no outside course can, though not always the Body of Knowledge or open-book technique.
  • Self-paced online study with instructor Q&A. This is the Atlantis format. It suits rotating shifts, contract work that moves between Oregon, Lima and other regions, and anyone who needs to repeat the calculations several times before they stick.

Whichever you choose, check that the material follows the editions on your window's Publications Effectivity Sheet, that the practice questions are original rather than claimed exam items, and that the timed papers copy the real closed-book and open-book split. Atlantis is not an API-approved training provider; the certificate comes only from passing API's examination.

Sponsoring API 510 candidates from a Toledo-area plant or contractor

Owner-users and inspection contractors often prepare several people at once, for instance ahead of a contract that names API 510 inspectors or when experienced unit inspectors are nearing retirement. One enquiry can cover the group and fees are quoted on request. Eligibility stays personal, so check each person's documented experience before enrolling them, and expect each to apply to API and sit the exam individually. In the United States Atlantis performs UT, MT, PT and VT inspection and does not perform radiography; ultrasonic testing in Toledo describes that side of its work.

faq.q: Can I attend an API 510 class in person in Toledo?
faq.a: Not with Atlantis. There is no Atlantis classroom in the Toledo area, and the API 510 course is studied online at your own pace with an instructor answering your questions. Other providers run seminars on fixed dates, some in person elsewhere. Whatever preparation you use, the examination is sat in person at a Prometric test centre once API has accepted your application.

faq.q: Does an Ohio special inspector commission replace API 510, or the other way round?
faq.a: Neither replaces the other. An Ohio special inspector holds a National Board commission and an Ohio commission and makes the inspections the state rules require, either for an insurer or for an owner-user running an NB-371 inspection programme. API 510 is a private certification that refinery owner-users ask for in their own vessel programmes. Some inspectors in Ohio owner-user groups hold both.

faq.q: Are deaerators and condensate drums part of API 510 work at a Toledo refinery?
faq.a: Deaerators, condensate drums and blowdown vessels are unfired pressure vessels, so they usually sit in a refinery's API 510 programme, and boiler water and steam condensate corrosion (RP 571, 3.9) is on the current Body of Knowledge. The boilers themselves, steam drums included, are inspected under Ohio's boiler rules by a general or special inspector, at the intervals chapter 1301:3-5 sets.

faq.q: Is temper embrittlement on the API 510 exam?
faq.a: Not in the current Body of Knowledge. It lists fifteen RP 571 paragraphs, including high-temperature hydrogen attack, high-temperature H2/H2S corrosion, wet H2S damage and brittle fracture, but temper embrittlement is not one of them. It still matters on the chrome-moly reactors of Toledo-area hydrocrackers, so learn it for the job, and check the list again when you book a window.

faq.q: Are heat exchanger tubesheet calculations on the API 510 exam?
faq.a: No. The Body of Knowledge excludes tubesheet calculations and the Section VIII Part UHX rules. Exchangers still appear, though: ASME PCC-2 Article 312 on inspecting and repairing shell-and-tube exchangers is examined, and so is RP 572. Expect questions on inspection, plugging and repair practice rather than on design.

faq.q: I study engineering at the University of Toledo. Can my co-op count towards API 510?
faq.a: Possibly, but API decides. Its rules count pressure vessel experience gained while employed by or under contract with an authorized inspection agency, which includes an owner-user inspection group, and with a bachelor's degree you need one year of supervising or performing inspection. Keep a detailed log of any co-op inspection work and present it on your application.

faq.q: Where would a candidate from Lima sit the API 510 exam?
faq.a: At whichever Prometric test centre suits them. Prometric lists test centres in and around Toledo, and you choose one when you book after API accepts your application. Plan the drive, because the day itself runs to 7.5 hours with both halves of the examination.

faq.q: Can a Toledo-area inspection contractor enrol several API 510 candidates together?
faq.a: Yes. Send one enquiry with the number of candidates and the windows they are aiming at, and the quote covers the group. Each person studies at their own pace with access to the instructor, applies to API individually and sits the examination individually. Check each candidate's documented experience first, because API decides eligibility person by person.
